title: Types of APIs Explained Simply
intro: APIs are the backbone of modern applications. They help different software systems communicate and share data seamlessly.

slides.heading: REST API
slides.subtitle: The most widely used API type.
points: Uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
Lightweight and easy to use
Returns data mostly in JSON format

slides.heading: SOAP API
slides.subtitle: A protocol for secure, structured communication.
points: Uses XML format for messages
Highly secure with built-in error handling
Common in enterprise applications

slides.heading: GraphQL API
slides.subtitle: Ask for exactly the data you need.
points: Single endpoint for all queries
Client decides the response shape
Avoids over-fetching and under-fetching

slides.heading: WebSocket API
slides.subtitle: Two-way communication that stays open.
points: Persistent connection between client and server
Server can push data without a new request
Much lower latency than polling

slides.heading: gRPC API
slides.subtitle: Fast, typed communication between services.
points: Uses Protocol Buffers, not JSON
Much faster than REST for service-to-service calls
Strict, strongly-typed contracts

title: HTTP Status Codes You Must Know
intro: Every API response carries a status code. Knowing what they mean saves hours of debugging.

slides.heading: 2xx Success
slides.subtitle: The request worked as expected.
points: 200 OK — standard successful response
201 Created — a new resource was made
204 No Content — success, nothing to return

slides.heading: 3xx Redirection
slides.subtitle: The resource moved somewhere else.
points: 301 Moved Permanently — update your bookmarks
302 Found — temporary redirect
304 Not Modified — use your cached copy

slides.heading: 4xx Client Error
slides.subtitle: The request itself was the problem.
points: 400 Bad Request — malformed input
401 Unauthorized — you're not logged in
403 Forbidden — logged in, but not allowed
404 Not Found — the resource doesn't exist

slides.heading: 5xx Server Error
slides.subtitle: The request was fine, the server wasn't.
points: 500 Internal Server Error — something crashed
502 Bad Gateway — upstream server failed
503 Service Unavailable — server is overloaded

cta: Which status code do you see the most in your logs?

title: SQL JOINs Explained Simply
intro: JOINs combine rows from two or more tables. Pick the wrong one and you either lose data or duplicate it.

slides.heading: INNER JOIN
slides.subtitle: Only rows that match in both tables.
points: Returns rows where the join condition is true in both tables
Rows with no match on either side are excluded
The most commonly used join
examples: Orders that have a matching customer

slides.heading: LEFT JOIN
slides.subtitle: Everything from the left table, matched or not.
points: Keeps all rows from the left table
Unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL
Useful for finding what's missing
examples: All customers, even those with zero orders

slides.heading: RIGHT JOIN
slides.subtitle: The mirror image of LEFT JOIN.
points: Keeps all rows from the right table
Unmatched left-side columns come back as NULL
Rarely used — most people rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN
examples: All products, even unordered ones, from the orders table

slides.heading: FULL JOIN
slides.subtitle: Everything from both tables.
points: Combines LEFT and RIGHT JOIN results
Unmatched rows from either side get NULLs
Good for finding mismatches between two tables
examples: Reconciling two systems that should be in sync

title: Git Commands Every Developer Needs
intro: You don't need 100 git commands memorized. These cover 90% of daily work.

slides.heading: Starting out
slides.subtitle: Get a project under version control.
points: git init — start tracking a new project
git clone <url> — copy an existing repo
git status — see what's changed

slides.heading: Saving work
slides.subtitle: Record changes as commits.
points: git add <file> — stage a change
git commit -m "message" — save staged changes
git push — send commits to the remote

slides.heading: Branching
slides.subtitle: Work on features without breaking main.
points: git switch -c <name> — create and move to a new branch
git switch <name> — move to an existing branch
git merge <name> — bring a branch's changes in

slides.heading: Undoing things
slides.subtitle: Mistakes happen, git can fix most of them.
points: git restore <file> — discard uncommitted changes
git reset --soft HEAD~1 — undo last commit, keep changes
git revert <commit> — safely undo a pushed commit

title: Web Security Basics Every Dev Should Know
intro: Most breaches don't come from genius hackers — they come from skipped basics. Start here.

slides.heading: SQL Injection
slides.subtitle: Untrusted input treated as executable SQL.
points: Happens when queries are built with string concatenation
An attacker can read or delete your entire database
Fixed with parameterized queries, never string building

slides.heading: XSS
slides.subtitle: Malicious scripts injected into your pages.
points: Happens when user input is rendered as raw HTML
Can steal cookies, sessions, and user data
Fixed by escaping output and using a strict CSP

slides.heading: CSRF
slides.subtitle: Tricking a logged-in user into an unwanted action.
points: Exploits the browser automatically sending cookies
Victim's own session is used against them
Fixed with CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies

slides.heading: Broken Auth
slides.subtitle: Weaknesses in login and session handling.
points: Weak password rules make brute-forcing easy
Tokens that never expire stay valid forever if leaked
Fixed with rate limiting, hashing, and short-lived tokens

title: How Caching Actually Works
intro: Caching is the single biggest lever for making an app feel fast. Here's how it's layered in a real system.

slides.heading: Browser Cache
slides.subtitle: The data never leaves the user's device.
points: Controlled by Cache-Control and ETag headers
Fastest possible response: zero network time
Best for static assets like images, CSS, JS

slides.heading: CDN Cache
slides.subtitle: A copy stored close to the user.
points: Edge servers around the world cache responses
Cuts latency by avoiding your origin server entirely
Great for content that's the same for every user

slides.heading: Application Cache
slides.subtitle: In-memory store like Redis sitting in front of your database.
points: Much faster than querying the database every time
Needs an invalidation strategy or data goes stale
Usually has a TTL as a safety net

slides.heading: Database Cache
slides.subtitle: The database's own internal optimizations.
points: Query plans and recently read pages are kept in memory
You don't control it directly, but indexes help it a lot
Still the slowest layer in this whole chain
examples: Hot rows in a popular table

title: The JavaScript Event Loop, Simply
intro: JavaScript is single-threaded, yet handles thousands of operations without freezing. This is how.

slides.heading: Call Stack
slides.subtitle: Where your code actually executes.
points: Functions are pushed on when called, popped off when done
Only one thing runs at a time here
A long-running function here blocks everything else

slides.heading: Web APIs
slides.subtitle: Where async work actually happens.
points: Timers, network requests and DOM events run outside the stack
Provided by the browser or Node, not JS itself
They report back once finished, not immediately

slides.heading: Microtask Queue
slides.subtitle: The high-priority line for promises.
points: Holds resolved Promise callbacks and queueMicrotask
Always fully drained before the next macrotask runs
This is why a resolved promise logs before a timer

slides.heading: Macrotask Queue
slides.subtitle: Where the next 'turn' of work waits.
points: Holds timers, I/O callbacks, and UI events
Only one macrotask runs per loop iteration
Runs only after the stack and microtasks are empty

cta: Did you know microtasks always run before the next timer?

title: Code Review Habits That Make You Look Senior
intro: The difference between a junior and senior PR often isn't the code — it's these habits.

slides.heading: Self-review first
slides.subtitle: Read your own diff before requesting review.
points: Catches typos and leftover console.logs
Lets you add context comments on tricky parts
Shows reviewers you respect their time

slides.heading: Small PRs
slides.subtitle: Easier to review means faster to merge.
points: Split unrelated changes into separate PRs
A 100-line PR gets reviewed same-day, a 1000-line one doesn't
Smaller diffs mean fewer missed bugs

slides.heading: Clear descriptions
slides.subtitle: Explain the why, not just the what.
points: Link the ticket or issue being solved
Mention tradeoffs you considered and rejected
Add a test plan so reviewers know how to verify it
examples: PR template with context + test plan

slides.heading: Respond fast
slides.subtitle: Momentum matters more than perfection.
points: Reply to review comments within a day, not a week
Disagree directly in comments, don't go silent
Thank reviewers for catching real issues
examples: Addressing comments same day they're posted

title: Frontend vs Backend vs Full Stack
intro: Three job titles you'll see everywhere. Here's what each one actually does, in plain language.

slides.heading: Frontend
slides.subtitle: Everything the user sees and touches.
points: Built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript
Frameworks like React, Vue or Angular
Cares about UI, accessibility and speed

slides.heading: Backend

points: Built with Node.js, Python, Java, Go and more

points: Builds features end to end
Broad skills, usually deeper on one side

title: CSS Flexbox vs Grid, Explained Simply
intro: Both are for layout, but they solve different problems. Knowing which to reach for saves a lot of frustration.

slides.heading: Flexbox
slides.subtitle: Layout in one direction: a row or a column.
points: Add display: flex to the parent
justify-content aligns along the main axis
align-items aligns along the cross axis

slides.heading: Grid
slides.subtitle: Layout in two directions: rows and columns.
points: Add display: grid to the parent
grid-template-columns defines the columns
gap adds space between items

slides.heading: When to use which
slides.subtitle: A simple rule of thumb.
points: Items in a single line? Use Flexbox
Rows and columns together? Use Grid
They work great combined
examples: Grid for the page, Flexbox inside each card

slides.heading: Centering, solved
slides.subtitle: The classic beginner question.
points: Flexbox: justify-content and align-items: center
Grid: place-items: center
Both center horizontally and vertically

title: Async JavaScript: Callbacks, Promises, async/await
intro: Async code lets JavaScript wait for slow things, like network requests, without freezing the page.

slides.heading: Callbacks
slides.subtitle: Pass a function to run later.
points: The original way to handle async work
Deep nesting leads to "callback hell"
Error handling gets messy fast

slides.heading: Promises
slides.subtitle: An object for a value that arrives later.
points: States: pending, fulfilled or rejected
Chain with .then() and .catch()
Promise.all runs tasks in parallel

slides.heading: async / await
slides.subtitle: Promise code that reads like normal code.
points: async functions always return a Promise
await pauses until the Promise settles
Use try/catch to handle errors

slides.heading: Common mistakes
slides.subtitle: Bugs almost everyone hits once.
points: Forgetting await and getting a Promise back
Awaiting independent calls one by one
No .catch() or try/catch for failures

title: Authentication vs Authorization
intro: They sound alike but answer two different questions. Mixing them up is a common source of security bugs.

slides.heading: Authentication
slides.subtitle: Who are you?
points: Verifies a user's identity
Passwords, one-time codes, passkeys or social login
Always happens before authorization

slides.heading: Authorization
slides.subtitle: What are you allowed to do?
points: Checks permissions after login
Often role-based: admin, editor, viewer
Must be enforced on the server

slides.heading: Sessions
slides.subtitle: The server remembers who you are.
points: Server stores the session, browser keeps an ID cookie
Easy to log a user out by deleting the session
Classic choice for server-rendered apps

slides.heading: JWT
slides.subtitle: A signed token the client carries.
points: Holds user info signed by the server
Can be verified without a database lookup
Hard to revoke, so keep expiry short

title: Big O Notation Explained Simply
intro: Big O describes how your code slows down as the input grows. It's the language every coding interview uses.

slides.heading: What is Big O?
slides.subtitle: How work grows as input grows.
points: Describes how time or memory scales
Ignores constants, focuses on growth
Usually describes the worst case
examples: Comparing two ways to solve a problem

slides.heading: O(1) Constant
slides.subtitle: Same time no matter the size.
points: Reading an array item by its index
Looking up a key in a hash map (on average)

slides.heading: O(n) Linear
slides.subtitle: Work grows with the input.
points: Looping through every item once
Double the input, roughly double the time
examples: Finding the max in an array

slides.heading: O(log n)
slides.subtitle: Halve the problem at every step.
points: Binary search on a sorted array
1 million items takes about 20 steps

slides.heading: O(n²) Quadratic
slides.subtitle: Nested loops over the same data.
points: Compares every item with every other item
Gets slow quickly on large inputs
Often fixable with a hash map

title: Docker Basics Every Developer Should Know
intro: Docker packages your app with everything it needs, so it runs the same on every machine.

slides.heading: What is Docker?
slides.subtitle: Apps in portable, isolated boxes.
points: Runs apps in isolated containers
Same environment on every machine
Ends "it works on my machine"

slides.heading: Image vs Container
slides.subtitle: The recipe vs the running dish.

One image can start many containers

title: REST API Design Best Practices
intro: A well-designed API is easy to guess, easy to use and hard to misuse. These conventions get you most of the way.

slides.heading: Use nouns
slides.subtitle: Resources in URLs, not actions.
points: GET /users, not GET /getUsers
Plural nouns for collections
Nest related data: /users/42/orders

slides.heading: HTTP methods
slides.subtitle: Let the method describe the action.
points: GET reads data
POST creates something new
PUT replaces, PATCH updates part of it
DELETE removes it

slides.heading: Status codes
slides.subtitle: Tell the client what happened.
points: 201 after creating a resource
400 for invalid input
404 when it doesn't exist
Never return 200 with an error inside

slides.heading: Version & paginate
slides.subtitle: Plan for growth from day one.
points: Version your API: /api/v1/
Paginate big lists: ?page=2&limit=20
Keep response shapes consistent

slides.heading: useState

Calling the setter re-renders the component

slides.heading: useEffect
slides.subtitle: Sync with things outside React.
points: Runs after the component renders
The dependency array controls when it re-runs
Return a cleanup function when needed

slides.heading: useRef
slides.subtitle: Keep a value without re-rendering.
points: Access DOM elements directly
Store values that survive re-renders
Changing .current doesn't re-render

slides.heading: useMemo & useCallback

useCallback caches a function

title: The CSS Box Model Explained Simply
intro: Every element on a web page is a rectangular box. Understanding its layers fixes most spacing bugs.

slides.heading: Content
slides.subtitle: The text or image itself.
points: Sized with width and height
The innermost layer of the box

slides.heading: Padding
slides.subtitle: Space inside the border.
points: Pushes content away from the border
Shows the element's background color

slides.heading: Border
slides.subtitle: The line around the padding.
points: Set with a width, style and color

slides.heading: Margin
slides.subtitle: Space outside the border.
points: Pushes other elements away
Always transparent
Vertical margins can collapse into one

slides.heading: box-sizing
slides.subtitle: The one line most projects add.

box-sizing: border-box includes them
Makes element sizes predictable

title: CSS Units: px vs rem vs em vs %
intro: Picking the right unit makes your layout scale nicely across screens and respect users' font settings.

slides.heading: px
slides.subtitle: A fixed size.
points: Same size regardless of the parent
Good for borders and fine details
Doesn't scale with the user's font settings

slides.heading: rem
slides.subtitle: Relative to the root font size.
points: 1rem equals the html font size (16px by default)
Scales when users change their browser font size
A great default for font sizes and spacing

slides.heading: em
slides.subtitle: Relative to the parent's font size.
points: Compounds when elements are nested
Handy for padding that scales with text

slides.heading: % and vw / vh
slides.subtitle: Relative to a container or the screen.
points: % is relative to the parent element
1vw is 1% of the viewport width
1vh is 1% of the viewport height

scenario.situation: A user with low vision sets their browser's default font size to 24px.
scenario.problem: Your site uses font-size: 14px everywhere, so the text stays tiny and hard to read.
scenario.fix: Switch font sizes to rem (14px becomes 0.875rem). The text now scales with the user's setting.
scenario.takeaway: Use rem for text so it respects user preferences.

title: var vs let vs const in JavaScript
intro: Three ways to declare a variable, each with different rules. Modern code mostly uses const and let.

slides.heading: var
slides.subtitle: The old way.
points: Function-scoped, not block-scoped
Hoisted and starts as undefined
Can be redeclared, which hides bugs

slides.heading: let
slides.subtitle: For values that change.
points: Block-scoped: lives inside { }
Can be reassigned
Can't be used before it's declared

slides.heading: const
slides.subtitle: For values that won't be reassigned.
points: Block-scoped, just like let
Can't be reassigned
Objects and arrays inside can still change

slides.heading: Rule of thumb
slides.subtitle: What most teams do.
points: Use const by default
Switch to let when you need to reassign
Avoid var in new code

scenario.situation: You loop with var i from 0 to 2 and start a setTimeout inside that logs i.
scenario.problem: It logs 3, 3, 3. var creates one shared i, which is already 3 when the timers fire.
scenario.fix: Change var to let. Each loop iteration gets its own i, so it logs 0, 1, 2.
scenario.takeaway: let and const are block-scoped; var is not.

title: JavaScript Array Methods You'll Use Daily
intro: These built-in methods replace most manual for-loops and make your code easier to read.

slides.heading: map()
slides.subtitle: Transform every item.
points: Returns a new array of the same length
Doesn't change the original array
examples: Users to a list of names

slides.heading: filter()
slides.subtitle: Keep only the matching items.
points: Returns a new array
Keeps items where the callback returns true

slides.heading: find()
slides.subtitle: Get the first match.
points: Returns the first matching item
Returns undefined if nothing matches
examples: Looking up a user by ID

slides.heading: reduce()
slides.subtitle: Boil an array down to one value.
points: Carries an accumulator through each item
Always pass a starting value

slides.heading: some() & every()
slides.subtitle: Yes-or-no questions about an array.
points: some: does at least one item match?
every: do all items match?

scenario.situation: An online store needs the total price of the in-stock items in a cart.
scenario.problem: A manual for-loop with if checks and a running total is long and easy to get wrong.
scenario.fix: cart.filter(i => i.inStock).reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0) does it in one readable line.
scenario.takeaway: Chain filter and reduce instead of hand-written loops.

title: == vs === and Truthy vs Falsy
intro: Two JavaScript quirks behind many beginner bugs. Here's how to stay out of trouble.

slides.heading: == (loose)
slides.subtitle: Converts types before comparing.
points: 0 == "" is true
null == undefined is true
The conversion rules are easy to forget

slides.heading: === (strict)
slides.subtitle: No type conversion.
points: Type and value must both match
0 === "" is false
Predictable, so use it by default

slides.heading: Falsy values
slides.subtitle: The main values that count as false.
points: false, 0 and "" (empty string)
null, undefined and NaN
Almost everything else is truthy

slides.heading: Watch out
slides.subtitle: Common surprises.
points: [] and {} are truthy, even when empty
The strings "0" and "false" are truthy
Check array.length when testing for empty

scenario.situation: A form checks if (quantity == 0) to show an "out of stock" warning.
scenario.problem: An empty input gives "", and "" == 0 is true, so the warning appears before the user types anything.
scenario.fix: Check for an empty value first, then compare Number(quantity) === 0. Only a real 0 shows the warning.
scenario.takeaway: Use === and convert types on purpose.

title: Git Merge vs Rebase, Explained Simply
intro: Both bring changes from one branch into another. They just leave behind a different history.

slides.heading: git merge
slides.subtitle: Join two histories together.
points: Creates a merge commit
Keeps the full branch history
Safe to use on shared branches

slides.heading: git rebase
slides.subtitle: Replay your commits on top.
points: Moves your commits onto the latest base
Produces a straight, linear history
Rewrites your commit IDs
examples: Updating a feature branch with main

slides.heading: The golden rule
slides.subtitle: Never rebase shared history.
points: Rebase only branches nobody else uses
Rewriting pushed commits breaks teammates' copies
If you must push, use --force-with-lease

slides.heading: Which to use?
slides.subtitle: A simple default.
points: Updating your own branch: rebase
Bringing a feature into main: merge
Follow your team's convention

scenario.situation: Your feature branch is three days old, and main has moved ahead with your teammates' work.
scenario.problem: Merging main in again and again fills your PR with noisy "Merge branch main" commits.
scenario.fix: Since only you use the branch, run git rebase main. Your commits now sit cleanly on top of the latest main.
scenario.takeaway: Rebase your own branches; merge shared ones.

cta: Team merge or team rebase?

title: npm Basics Every JavaScript Developer Needs
intro: npm installs and manages the packages your JavaScript projects depend on. Here's what you need day to day.

slides.heading: package.json
slides.subtitle: Your project's ID card.
points: Lists the name, version and scripts
Lists the packages you depend on
Create one with npm init -y

slides.heading: Installing
slides.subtitle: Adding packages to a project.
points: npm install express adds a dependency
npm install -D eslint adds a dev dependency
npm install alone installs everything listed

slides.heading: Lock file
slides.subtitle: package-lock.json
points: Records the exact installed versions
Makes installs repeatable on every machine
Commit it to git

slides.heading: Scripts
slides.subtitle: Shortcuts for common tasks.
points: Defined under "scripts" in package.json
Run them with npm run dev or npm run build
npm start and npm test work without run

slides.heading: node_modules
slides.subtitle: Where packages are installed.
points: Can get very large
Never commit it to git
Delete and reinstall to fix odd issues

scenario.situation: Your app works on your laptop, but the CI build fails with an error inside a dependency.
scenario.problem: No lock file was committed, so CI installed a newer version of a package that has a bug.
scenario.fix: Commit package-lock.json and use npm ci in CI. Every machine now installs the exact same versions.
scenario.takeaway: Commit the lock file; use npm ci in CI.

cta: How big is your biggest node_modules folder?

title: Environment Variables and Secrets 101
intro: API keys and passwords should never live in your code. Environment variables keep them separate and safe.

slides.heading: What they are
slides.subtitle: Settings that live outside your code.
points: Key-value pairs set in the environment
Read in Node.js with process.env.NAME
Different values per environment

slides.heading: .env files
slides.subtitle: Local secrets for development.
points: One KEY=value per line
Loaded by dotenv or node --env-file
Add .env to your .gitignore

slides.heading: Never commit secrets
slides.subtitle: Git history remembers everything.
points: Deleting the file later doesn't erase history
Bots scan public repos for leaked keys
If a key leaks, revoke it and make a new one

slides.heading: In production
slides.subtitle: Where secrets should live.
points: Your hosting provider's environment settings
CI secrets, like GitHub Actions secrets
A secrets manager for larger teams

scenario.situation: A developer hard-codes a cloud API key in config.js and pushes it to a public GitHub repo.
scenario.problem: Bots scan public repos for keys. Someone finds it and runs up charges on the account.
scenario.fix: Revoke the key, put the new one in an environment variable, add .env to .gitignore and read it with process.env.
scenario.takeaway: Secrets go in environment variables, never in code.

cta: Have you ever accidentally committed a secret?

title: CORS Errors Explained Simply
intro: Seen "blocked by CORS policy" in your console? Here's what's actually happening and how to fix it.

slides.heading: Same-origin policy
slides.subtitle: The browser's default rule.
points: Origin = protocol + domain + port
Pages can't read responses from other origins by default
It protects users from malicious sites

slides.heading: What CORS is
slides.subtitle: A way for servers to opt in.
points: The server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin
The browser checks it before sharing the response
The server decides, not the frontend

slides.heading: Preflight requests
slides.subtitle: The browser asks first.
points: An OPTIONS request sent before some requests
Triggered by methods like PUT or custom headers
The server must reply with what it allows

slides.heading: How to fix it
slides.subtitle: Fix it on the server.
points: Configure CORS in your backend
Allow specific origins, especially with cookies
Use a dev-server proxy during local development

scenario.situation: Your React app on localhost:5173 calls your API on localhost:3000.
scenario.problem: The browser blocks the response with a CORS error, even though the same request works in Postman.
scenario.fix: Allow that origin on the API, for example in Express: app.use(cors({ origin: "http://localhost:5173" })).
scenario.takeaway: CORS is fixed on the server, not the frontend.

cta: How many hours has CORS cost you?

title: Cookies vs localStorage vs sessionStorage
intro: Three ways to store data in the browser, each built for a different job.

slides.heading: Cookies
slides.subtitle: Small data sent with requests.
points: About 4KB per cookie
Sent to the server automatically
Can be httpOnly so JavaScript can't read them

slides.heading: localStorage
slides.subtitle: Browser storage that persists.
points: Around 5MB per site in most browsers
Stays until it's cleared
Readable by any script on the page

slides.heading: sessionStorage
slides.subtitle: Storage for a single tab.
points: Same API as localStorage
Cleared when the tab closes
Not shared between tabs

slides.heading: Security tip
slides.subtitle: Choose storage carefully.
points: Never store passwords in the browser
Prefer httpOnly cookies for auth tokens
Treat stored data as user-editable

scenario.situation: An app stores the user's login token in localStorage.
scenario.problem: An XSS bug lets an injected script read localStorage and send the token to an attacker.
scenario.fix: Keep the session in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie. JavaScript can't read it, so XSS can't steal it.
scenario.takeaway: Keep auth tokens out of JavaScript's reach.

cta: Where do you store auth tokens in your apps?

title: SQL vs NoSQL Databases Explained
intro: Both store data, but in very different ways. The right choice depends on your data and how you read it.

slides.heading: SQL databases
slides.subtitle: Tables with a fixed schema.
points: Rows and columns, like a spreadsheet
Relationships through joins
Strong consistency with transactions

slides.heading: NoSQL databases
slides.subtitle: Flexible data models.
points: Document, key-value, graph or wide-column
Schema can change easily
Often built to scale across many servers

slides.heading: Pick SQL when
slides.subtitle: Structure and correctness matter.
points: Your data is highly related
Correctness is critical, like payments
You need complex queries and reports

slides.heading: Pick NoSQL when
slides.subtitle: Flexibility and scale matter.
points: The data shape changes often
You mostly read data by a single key
You need very high write volume

scenario.situation: A team builds a banking app on a document database because it felt quicker to start.
scenario.problem: A transfer updates two accounts, and keeping both balances consistent becomes complicated and error-prone.
scenario.fix: Use a relational database with transactions. Both updates succeed together or fail together.
scenario.takeaway: Choose by your data and its rules, not by hype.

cta: SQL or NoSQL for your current project?

title: Database Indexes Explained Simply
intro: An index works like the index in a book: it lets the database find rows without reading every page.

slides.heading: Without an index
slides.subtitle: The database reads every row.
points: Called a full table scan
Gets slow as tables grow

slides.heading: With an index
slides.subtitle: Jump straight to the right rows.
points: Usually stored as a sorted B-tree
Lookups take a few steps, not millions
Speeds up WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY

slides.heading: The trade-off
slides.subtitle: Indexes aren't free.
points: Each index uses extra storage
Inserts and updates get slower
Index the columns you actually query

slides.heading: Check your query
slides.subtitle: Don't guess, measure.
points: Run EXPLAIN to see the query plan
A full scan on a big table hints at a missing index
CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users (email);

scenario.situation: Your login query, SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?, gets slower as the app reaches a million users.
scenario.problem: There's no index on email, so the database scans every row on every single login.
scenario.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email); lets the database jump straight to the matching row.
scenario.takeaway: Index the columns you search by.

cta: Have you ever fixed a slow query with one index?

title: Core Web Vitals Explained Simply
intro: Google's three metrics for how fast and smooth your page feels to real users.

slides.heading: LCP
slides.subtitle: Largest Contentful Paint: loading.
points: Time until the main content appears
Good: 2.5 seconds or less
Fix: optimize images, use a CDN

slides.heading: INP
slides.subtitle: Interaction to Next Paint: responsiveness.
points: How fast the page responds to clicks and taps
Good: 200 milliseconds or less
Fix: break up long JavaScript tasks

slides.heading: CLS
slides.subtitle: Cumulative Layout Shift: stability.
points: How much the layout jumps while loading
Good: 0.1 or less
Fix: set image sizes, reserve space for ads

slides.heading: Measure it
slides.subtitle: Free tools to check your site.
points: Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools
PageSpeed Insights for real-user data
The web-vitals library for your own analytics

scenario.situation: A blog's mobile LCP is 4.8 seconds, well above the 2.5 second target.
scenario.problem: The hero image is a 3 MB PNG, so the main content takes a long time to appear.
scenario.fix: Convert it to WebP, size it for the screen and preload it. That alone can bring LCP under 2.5 seconds.
scenario.takeaway: Oversized images are a top cause of slow LCP.

cta: What's your site's LCP right now?

title: Web Accessibility Basics Every Dev Should Know
intro: Accessible sites work for everyone, including people using screen readers, keyboards or zoom.

slides.heading: Alt text
slides.subtitle: Describe your images.
points: Screen readers read alt text aloud
Describe the purpose, not just the look
Use alt="" for purely decorative images

slides.heading: Keyboard access
slides.subtitle: Not everyone uses a mouse.
points: Everything clickable works with Tab and Enter
Keep a visible focus outline
Use real <button> and <a> elements

slides.heading: Color contrast
slides.subtitle: Make text easy to read.
points: WCAG AA asks for 4.5:1 for normal text
Don't rely on color alone to show meaning
Test with a contrast checker

slides.heading: Forms
slides.subtitle: Where accessibility breaks most often.
points: Every input needs a <label>
Error messages should say how to fix it
Placeholder text is not a label

scenario.situation: A checkout form uses grey placeholder text instead of labels.
scenario.problem: Screen reader users can't tell what each field is, and the hint disappears as soon as anyone types.
scenario.fix: Add a visible <label for="email"> to every input, and keep placeholders for examples only.
scenario.takeaway: Every input needs a real label.

cta: Have you ever tried using your site with only a keyboard?

title: Why Developers Love TypeScript
intro: TypeScript is JavaScript with types. It catches many bugs before your code ever runs.

slides.heading: What it is
slides.subtitle: JavaScript plus a type system.
points: Compiles to plain JavaScript
Types are checked, then removed at build time
You can adopt it gradually

slides.heading: Basic types
slides.subtitle: The building blocks.
points: string, number and boolean
string[] for an array of strings
Unions: "admin" | "user"

slides.heading: Interfaces
slides.subtitle: Describe the shape of objects.
points: interface User { id: number; name: string }
Your editor autocompletes properties
Typos in property names become errors

slides.heading: Why it helps
slides.subtitle: Benefits you feel every day.
points: Catches bugs while you type
Makes refactoring much safer
Works as living documentation

scenario.situation: Your backend renames user.fullName to user.name.
scenario.problem: In plain JavaScript, every screen still reading fullName quietly shows undefined in production.
scenario.fix: With a User interface, update the type once and the compiler points to every line still using fullName.
scenario.takeaway: Types turn runtime surprises into compile errors.

cta: Do you write TypeScript or plain JavaScript?

title: Unit vs Integration vs E2E Testing
intro: Different tests catch different bugs. The testing pyramid shows how to balance them.

slides.heading: Unit tests
slides.subtitle: Test one small piece in isolation.
points: Fast and cheap to run
Test a single function or component
Should be most of your tests

slides.heading: Integration tests
slides.subtitle: Test pieces working together.
points: Check modules work correctly together
Often include a real database or API
Slower than unit tests
examples: An API endpoint with its database

slides.heading: E2E tests
slides.subtitle: Test the app like a real user.
points: Run in a real browser
Catch issues across the whole stack
Slowest and most fragile, so keep them few

slides.heading: The pyramid
slides.subtitle: How to balance them.
points: Many unit tests at the base
Fewer integration tests in the middle
A handful of E2E tests on top

scenario.situation: A refactor of the discount function accidentally breaks coupons above 50%.
scenario.problem: Nobody notices until customers start reporting wrong prices.
scenario.fix: A few unit tests for calculateDiscount() would have failed instantly, before the change was merged.
scenario.takeaway: Unit test your business logic first.

cta: Which kind of test do you write the most?

title: Responsive Design Basics
intro: Most visitors browse on phones. These basics make your site look good on every screen size.

slides.heading: Viewport meta tag
slides.subtitle: Step one for mobile.
points: Tells phones to use the device's real width
Without it, pages render zoomed out
Goes in the <head> of every page

slides.heading: Mobile first
slides.subtitle: Start small, then scale up.
points: Write base styles for small screens
Add min-width media queries for bigger ones
Usually leads to simpler CSS

slides.heading: Media queries
slides.subtitle: Change the layout at breakpoints.
points: @media (min-width: 768px) { ... }
Switch columns, sizes or visibility
Add breakpoints where your design breaks

slides.heading: Flexible media
slides.subtitle: Images that never overflow.
points: img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }
Use srcset to serve different image sizes
Prefer fluid widths over fixed pixels

scenario.situation: Your site looks perfect on desktop, but on a phone the text is tiny and users have to zoom.
scenario.problem: The viewport meta tag is missing, so the phone renders the page at desktop width and shrinks it.
scenario.fix: Add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> and build the layout mobile first.
scenario.takeaway: The viewport tag is step one for mobile.

cta: Do you design mobile first or desktop first?

title: Monolith vs Microservices, Explained
intro: Two ways to structure a backend. Neither is always better; it depends on your team and your stage.

slides.heading: Monolith
slides.subtitle: One codebase, deployed as one app.
points: Simple to build, test and deploy
Easy to debug in one place
Harder to scale parts independently

slides.heading: Microservices
slides.subtitle: Many small services working together.
points: Each service owns one job and its data
Teams can deploy independently
Adds network calls and operational complexity

slides.heading: Where to start
slides.subtitle: The usual advice.
points: Start with a well-organized monolith
Split out a service when a real need appears
Keep modules separated from day one

scenario.situation: A three-person startup splits its brand-new app into eight microservices.
scenario.problem: They spend more time on deployments, networking and cross-service bugs than on building features.
scenario.fix: Merge back into one modular monolith, and split out a service only when one part truly needs to scale alone.
scenario.takeaway: Start simple; split when there's a real reason.

cta: Monolith or microservices at your company?

title: How to Debug Like a Pro
intro: Debugging is a skill you can learn. This process works for almost any bug.

slides.heading: Read the error
slides.subtitle: It often tells you exactly what's wrong.
points: Read the whole message, not just the first line
The stack trace shows where it happened
Find the first line from your own code

slides.heading: Reproduce it
slides.subtitle: Make it happen on demand.
points: Find the exact steps that trigger it
Shrink it to the smallest failing case
A bug you can reproduce is half fixed

slides.heading: Use your tools
slides.subtitle: Stop guessing, start looking.
points: Set breakpoints in DevTools or your editor
Log values at key points
Check the Network tab for failed requests

slides.heading: Search smart
slides.subtitle: Someone has probably seen it before.
points: Search the exact error message
Check the official docs and GitHub issues
Explain the problem out loud, step by step

scenario.situation: Your app crashes with "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')".
scenario.problem: You start changing random code, hoping the error goes away.
scenario.fix: The stack trace points to your line. Logging the value shows the API returned nothing. Fix: (data ?? []).map(...).
scenario.takeaway: Read the error, find the line, check the value.

cta: What's the longest you've spent on a single bug?

title: What Is a Load Balancer?
intro: When one server isn't enough, a load balancer spreads traffic across many. It's a building block of almost every large app.

slides.heading: The problem
slides.subtitle: One server can't do it all.
points: Traffic grows beyond what one machine handles
One server is a single point of failure

slides.heading: The solution
slides.subtitle: Spread requests across servers.
points: Sits in front of your servers
Sends each request to a healthy server
Users still see one address

slides.heading: Strategies
slides.subtitle: How it picks a server.
points: Round robin: servers take turns
Least connections: pick the least busy
IP hash: same user, same server

slides.heading: Health checks
slides.subtitle: Routing around failures.
points: Checks each server regularly
Stops sending traffic to failing servers
Adds them back once they recover

scenario.situation: A product launch sends ten times the usual traffic to a site running on a single server.
scenario.problem: The server maxes out, requests time out, and the site goes down at the worst possible moment.
scenario.fix: Put a load balancer in front of several servers. Traffic is shared, and if one server fails the others keep serving.
scenario.takeaway: Scale out and remove single points of failure.

cta: Have you set up a load balancer before?

title: The 4 Pillars of Object-Oriented Programming
intro: OOP shows up in interviews and in languages like Java, Python and C#. Here are the four core ideas in plain words.

slides.heading: Encapsulation
slides.subtitle: Keep data and behavior together.
points: Bundle data with the methods that use it
Hide internal details behind a clear interface

slides.heading: Abstraction
slides.subtitle: Show only what matters.
points: Expose simple methods, hide the complexity
Like driving a car without knowing the engine

slides.heading: Inheritance
slides.subtitle: Reuse code from a parent class.
points: A child class extends a parent class
Shares behavior without copying it
Use it only for true "is-a" relationships

slides.heading: Polymorphism
slides.subtitle: One interface, many forms.
points: Different classes answer the same method
Code works with any object that fits

scenario.situation: A payment app supports cards and now needs UPI and PayPal too.
scenario.problem: One giant function with an if/else for every payment type gets harder to change with each new method.
scenario.fix: Create a Payment interface with pay(). Card, UPI and PayPal each implement it, and checkout just calls pay().
scenario.takeaway: Polymorphism lets you add new types without editing old code.

cta: Which pillar was hardest to understand at first?
